title: APPHIA: THE WOMAN WHO HEARD THE GOSPEL CHALLENGE THE CHAINS OF SLAVERY
paragraphs: APPHIA: THE WOMAN WHO HEARD THE GOSPEL CHALLENGE THE CHAINS OF SLAVERY

An enslaved man with an uncertain future. A household confronted by grace. A woman whose name was preserved in Scripture. And a letter that still challenges the way we treat people we believe no longer deserve another chance.
Imagine being in a room where someone is about to read a letter that could change another person's life forever.
Not because it contained money.
Not because it carried the authority of an earthly king.
But because it contained something that threatened the very foundations of human pride, social status, entitlement, and condemnation.
The Gospel of Jesus Christ.
There was a woman named Apphia.
You may have read past her name without ever stopping to wonder why the Holy Spirit allowed it to remain in Scripture.
She never delivered a recorded sermon. We have no record of her performing miracles. Scripture does not preserve a single sentence she spoke.
Yet her name appears in one of the most profoundly personal and socially challenging letters in the New Testament.
A letter concerning an enslaved man named Onesimus.
A letter about forgiveness that would cost something.
A letter about a relationship that could never remain the same once Christ became its center.
And perhaps, without realizing it, you need to hear that same letter today.
Because somewhere in your life, there may be an Onesimus you still refuse to forgive.
Or perhaps you are the Onesimus who wonders whether anyone will ever see you as something more than your worst mistake.
Paul begins his letter with these words:

“Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer, And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house.”
— Philemon 1–2, KJV
In the Greek text used by most modern critical editions of the New Testament, Apphia is addressed as:
Ἀπφίᾳ τῇ ἀδελφῇ — Apphia tē adelphē
Literally, “to Apphia, the sister.”
The word ἀδελφή (adelphē) means sister and, in this Christian context, expresses spiritual kinship within the family of believers.
Paul recognized Apphia as a sister in Christ.
Not merely as someone standing in the background of another person's story.
Not as someone whose spiritual identity depended entirely upon a man's position.
She was individually named in an apostolic letter addressed to fellow believers and a household church.

Some interpreters have suggested that Apphia may have been Philemon's wife, possibly sharing responsibilities within the household. That is a reasonable historical possibility, but Scripture never explicitly confirms their relationship.
We must never turn an interesting possibility into a biblical certainty.
What we do know is powerful enough.
Apphia was among the named recipients of a letter confronting how a Christian household should receive an enslaved man who had become a brother in Christ.
His name was Onesimus.
His Greek name, Ὀνήσιμος (Onēsimos), carries the meaning of useful, beneficial, or profitable.
Yet Paul describes him as someone who had formerly been unprofitable to Philemon.

Many readers understand Onesimus to have been a runaway enslaved man. That is a longstanding interpretation of the letter, although Scripture does not explicitly describe the circumstances of his departure or establish that he committed theft.
What is clear is that Onesimus had been separated from Philemon, had encountered Paul during his imprisonment, and had undergone a profound spiritual transformation.
Paul writes:
— Philemon 10–11, KJV
Notice what Paul calls him.
My son.
Not my problem.
Not my inconvenience.
Not a worthless man.
Not someone beyond redemption.
My son.
In Greek, Paul uses the expression τοῦ ἐμοῦ τέκνου (tou emou teknou) — “my child.”
Paul was describing a spiritual relationship formed through the Gospel during his imprisonment.
The world knew Onesimus according to his social position.
Paul knew him according to his relationship in Christ.
What a devastatingly beautiful difference.
Have you ever been introduced by your failures instead of your name?
Have you ever felt that no matter how much you changed, someone would always remember the person you used to be?
The adulterer.
The addict.
The liar.
The prisoner.
The irresponsible parent.
The disgraced Christian.
The person who disappointed everyone.
Perhaps you have genuinely repented. Perhaps you have cried before God in the darkness, asking Him to rebuild what sin destroyed.
But people still speak about you as though your transformation never happened.
They remember your scandal.
Jesus knows what His grace can accomplish in your life.
That does not mean repentance eliminates every earthly consequence. It does not mean broken trust is immediately restored or that accountability becomes unnecessary.
Grace does something deeper.
It refuses to make your sin the final definition of your identity when you have been reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
“If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature,” Paul declares in 2 Corinthians 5:17.
The Gospel does not merely teach broken people how to appear respectable.
It makes spiritually dead people alive in Christ.
And now Paul was sending Onesimus back.
But listen carefully to how he describes him:
“Whom I have sent again: thou therefore receive him, that is, mine own bowels.”
— Philemon 12, KJV
The older English expression “mine own bowels” can sound strange to modern readers.
The Greek expression is τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα (ta ema splanchna).
Literally referring to one's inward organs, the expression was used figuratively for deep affection, compassion, and tender emotional attachment.
In contemporary English, Paul is essentially saying:
I am sending you my very heart.
Let that sink in.
An enslaved man whom society could regard primarily as another person's property had become someone Paul described as his own heart.
This is what the Gospel does when it reaches beyond our mouths and penetrates our relationships.
It changes how we see people.
It challenges the categories through which we assign human worth.
It confronts the pride that makes us believe another person's dignity depends upon their usefulness to us.
And Apphia was among those addressed in this extraordinary letter.
We do not know her reaction.
We cannot claim she wept, protested, welcomed Onesimus, or persuaded Philemon to release him. Scripture does not tell us what happened afterward.
But we know the words addressed to that household.
And those words still demand a response from ours.
“For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever; Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved.”
— Philemon 15–16, KJV
The Greek is astonishingly direct:
οὐκέτι ὡς δοῦλον ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ δοῦλον, ἀδελφὸν ἀγαπητόν
Ouketi hōs doulon all’ hyper doulon, adelphon agapēton.
“No longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother.”
The word δοῦλος (doulos) in this context refers to an enslaved person.
We should not soften the historical reality by pretending Onesimus was simply an employee who had resigned from his job.
Roman slavery involved profound inequalities of power and legal status. Enslaved people could experience exploitation, violence, and severe restrictions upon their freedom.
Paul's appeal must be understood against that background.

Although the letter does not explicitly record Onesimus's legal emancipation or announce a comprehensive abolition of Roman slavery, it confronts the relationship between Philemon and Onesimus with a radical Christian truth.
Onesimus was to be received as a beloved brother.
Not merely according to his former social standing.
Not merely according to what he could provide.
But as someone whose relationship with Christ demanded a fundamentally different relationship with fellow believers.
Galatians 3:28 reinforces this spiritual equality:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.”
The cross leaves no room for the arrogance that treats one human soul as inherently more valuable than another.
And here is where this ancient letter becomes painfully personal.
How many of us worship Jesus while treating people in ways that contradict His Gospel?
We sing about mercy but humiliate those who have failed.
We celebrate redemption but continually resurrect someone else's past.
We ask God to overlook our offenses while carefully documenting every offense committed against us.
We want our own story to be rewritten by grace while insisting that someone else's story remain permanently stained by scandal.
We want Jesus to be our Savior.
But we struggle to let Him become Lord over our resentment.
Perhaps the most uncomfortable thing about the letter to Philemon is that it was addressed not only to an individual but also to others within his Christian community.
Including Apphia.
The Gospel was not meant to remain a private religious sentiment.
It was meant to transform the household.
The relationships.
The exercise of authority.
The treatment of vulnerable people.
The way believers responded when someone who had once been separated from them returned as a brother in Christ.
What would happen if the Gospel truly entered your household today?
Would your children encounter a different version of you?
Would your spouse experience more humility instead of constant criticism?
Would the people who work for you discover that your Christianity extends beyond your Sunday worship?
Would someone you have repeatedly condemned finally encounter compassion?
Would your family recognize Jesus in the way you respond when you are disappointed?
Christianity becomes deeply uncomfortable when it moves from the pages of Scripture into the rooms where we exercise power over other people.
It is easier to post a Bible verse than to apologize.
Easier to defend sound doctrine than to admit our own hypocrisy.
Easier to demand repentance from others than to surrender our pride.
But Jesus did not die merely to improve our religious vocabulary.
He died to redeem sinners.
To reconcile us to God.
To transform our lives through His grace.
And then Paul writes something that beautifully echoes the heart of the Gospel:
“If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself. If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account.”
— Philemon 17–18, KJV
Put that on mine account.
The Greek expression is:
τοῦτο ἐμοὶ ἐλλόγα — touto emoi elloga.
“Charge this to me.”
Paul was willing to assume responsibility for any debt Onesimus might owe.
He did not simply tell Philemon to be compassionate from a comfortable distance.
He was willing to bear a personal cost.

And although Paul was not performing the saving work that belongs to Christ alone, his willingness to bear another person's debt offers a moving illustration of the sacrificial love Christians have received through Jesus.
At Calvary, Jesus did infinitely more.
He bore our sins.
He gave Himself for the unrighteous.
He endured the suffering through which sinners could be reconciled to God.
Isaiah 53:5 declares that He was wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our iniquities.
Colossians 2:13–14 describes God forgiving our trespasses and canceling the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross.
We could not purchase our redemption.
We could not erase our guilt through religious performance.
We could not make ourselves righteous through donations, achievements, reputation, or human approval.
Jesus accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
And when that truth finally penetrates your heart, something begins to change.
You stop looking at broken people as though you were never broken.
You stop speaking about sinners as though you never needed a Savior.
You stop treating mercy as something you deserve but others must earn.
You remember the cross.
Perhaps you needed this reminder today because you are exhausted from carrying the shame of who you used to be.
You have convinced yourself that God could forgive everyone except you.
You have sat in church feeling like an outsider.
You have smiled in photographs while privately wondering whether your life will ever become something beautiful again.
Hear this.
Your sin is serious.
But Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Your past may contain chapters you wish had never been written.
But your past does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
Confess your sins.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Trust in His finished work.
Walk in repentance, obedience, and faith.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness when we confess them.
And perhaps you are reading this from the other side of the story.
Someone hurt you.
Someone betrayed your trust.
Someone left you carrying consequences you never deserved.
The Gospel's call to forgiveness does not require you to tolerate abuse, abandon wise boundaries, conceal wrongdoing, or immediately restore trust to someone who remains dangerous.
Forgiveness is not pretending that evil never happened.
Reconciliation requires truth, repentance, and appropriate accountability.
But you do not have to spend the remainder of your life allowing another person's wrongdoing to govern your heart.
Bring your wounds to Jesus.
Let Him teach you what mercy looks like without sacrificing truth.
Let Him loosen the grip of bitterness without asking you to deny your pain.
Let Him become Lord even over the parts of your story you still struggle to discuss.
Perhaps your struggle is shame.
Perhaps it is unforgiveness.
Perhaps it is the pride that has prevented you from admitting how deeply you need grace.
You do not have to publicly disclose your wounds. But those few words may become a meaningful expression of your desire for Christ to transform you.
And when you see someone else commenting, remember that behind that name is a human being with a story you may know nothing about.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Let it become an opportunity for believers to carry one another's burdens.
Your simple act of sharing could place biblical encouragement before someone who desperately needs it.
That is one meaningful way to participate in spreading the Gospel.
Throughout Scripture, believers are encouraged to support those who labor in teaching and sharing God's Word.

Galatians 6:6 teaches that those receiving instruction in the Word should share good things with those who teach them. First Corinthians 9:14 affirms the principle of supporting those who proclaim the Gospel.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving must come willingly from the heart, not through pressure or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
If you are prayerfully considering how to allocate your Christian giving, you may choose to include this ministry within your offerings, according to your convictions and responsibilities.
It is helping us continue the work of communicating biblical truth, encouraging spiritual growth, and pointing people toward the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
You cannot purchase God's favor.
You cannot buy salvation.
But when God has given you the willingness and ability to support Gospel-centered work, generosity can become one beautiful expression of your worship.
Give willingly. Share generously. Pray faithfully. And above all, glorify Jesus Christ.
Nearly two thousand years ago, a woman named Apphia was addressed in a letter concerning an enslaved man named Onesimus.
Her name occupies only a small portion of Scripture.
Yet the message delivered to that household continues to confront every generation of believers.
Will we see people only through the lens of their past?
Will we use our position to diminish others?
Will we preach a Gospel of grace while refusing to practice its implications?
Or will we remember that we, too, stood in desperate need of mercy?
Onesimus was described as formerly unprofitable.
Then he was called a son.
A beloved brother.
Paul's very heart.
What a remarkable testimony to the transforming power of the Gospel.
The world may remember where you fell.
People may remember what you lost.
Your enemies may remember what you did.
But when you come to Jesus in repentance and faith, your condemnation is not the final word.
Christ is.
Never turn someone's yesterday into a prison when the Savior you worship gave His life to redeem sinners.
